newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - API data to show exports cut heat build.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - API data to show exports cut heat build.

text.p: Heating oil stocks are expected to show a bullishly low build in Tuesday evening's American Petroleum Institute (API) report, as exports to Europe contained the build and provide the next chapter to the low heating oil supply story in the United States and abroad.
"The feeling is that there are plenty of exports coming out of the Gulf, and more of it is possible," said Tom Bentz, an analyst with ING Derivatives.
A Reuters survey shows distillate stocks, of which heating oil is a component, growing 1.6 million barrels.
The estimate ranged between 0.7 million and three million.

Crude stocks were seen unchanged to down 2.5 million barrels as refinery utilization rates were expected to remain a lofty 95 percent. High runs reflected increased distillate production, traders said.

Talk of gasoline imports from Europe has stoked concerns of oversupply, but dealers expect imports to show up in next week's data on the notion that cargoes had not yet arrived in time to be reflected this week. Tonight's data reflects stocks as of September 20. Consequently, gasoline inventories were seen unchanged to one million higher.
"I am not putting too much stock in the import talk since it is only anecdotal at this point," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group.
"With heating oil, we may be competing with Europe (for supplies), but in the end, world demand in general for heating oil is high," said Evans.
Analysts said the price of heating oil becomes attractive for export when heating oil is $1.50 a barrel below gas oil, Europe's equivalent of heating oil.
Last week, the difference hovered between $1.50 to $2.00.
"I would say that was pretty tempting (for exports)," said Linda Abramo, an analyst with Energy Security Analysis Inc.
Analysts estimated that exports may have shaved off one million barrels from heating oil stocks.
Europe's need for U.S. heating oil will depend in part on the ability of the European market to adjust to new distillate specifications there, analysts said.

"If they have a hard time with them, we could see an increase in exports," said Rita Beale, an analyst with FIMAT USA Futures. Even without the export story, analysts noted that heating oil's fundamentals remain bullish.
According to last week's API data for the week ended September 13, heating oil stocks were 20.7 million barrels below a year ago.

Most of the shortfall is in northeastern United States, the world's largest market for heating oil. Total distillate stocks, which also includes diesel fuel, were 21.5 million barrels below a year ago.
